records.text: An anonymous senior police-department source said only a district attorney could authorize the release of evidence such as Charlie Kirk's necklace and microphone, and that such a release would require a signature.
records.speaker: Anonymous Source #7 (Ep sKuYLNx3iRo)

appearances.snippet: Also, I wanted to add here: someone emailed us with very good knowledge. Like, we'll just say this person was very high up the chain at a police department. He said— ... You should be able to find what district attorney, because only a district attorney could release that, like the cross necklace, the back to Erika (Erika Kirk), the microphone that would require a signed release from a district attorney that never happens. It is considered evidence unless a district attorney signs off on it.

verification.notes: Current Utah sources support that evidence release generally requires authorization and that a prosecuting attorney may authorize or petition for release in some circumstances. The claim that only a district attorney can authorize every release is too broad: a Utah police evidence policy also permits authorization by the responsible officer, and state law assigns some transfers to a district court on a signed prosecutorial petition. The specific custodian and legal basis for the necklace and microphone were not established.

sources.title: Farmington City Police evidence release policy
sources.relevance: States that evidence may be released with authorization from the prosecuting attorney or responsible officer, contradicting the claim of exclusive district-attorney authority.

sources.title: Utah Code 24-2-105 transfer and sharing procedures
sources.relevance: Shows that some seized-property releases require a signed prosecutorial petition and district-court authorization.
